MINUTES
  ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  MARCH 8, 2021

CHAIR STEGURA called the meeting of the Environmental Advisory Committee of the City of
Rolling Hills Estates to order at 7:00 p.m.

2.  ROLL CALL

COMMITTEE MEMBERS PRESENT:  Stegura, Bacinski, Chan-Southwell, O’Malley,
  Radocchio, Schachter, Uppal, Wisot,

COMMITTEE MEMBERS ABSENT:  Bain, Larson

STAFF MEMBERS PRESENT:  Jeannie Naughton, Planning Manager
  Carol Corea, Administrative Assistant

ALSO PRESENT:  India Brookover, Project Manager, SCAG
  Laura Male, Project Manager, Sapphos Environmental
  Jonathan Cain, Sustainability Manager, Sapphos Environmental
  Ryan Johnson, Transportation Planner, Alta Planning

3.  APPROVAL OF MINUTES

A.  APPROVAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING, JUNE 3, 2020

COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER
O’MALLEY to,

  APPROVE THE ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING MINUTES OF
  AUGUST 19, 2020

There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

4.  AUDIENCE ITEMS/ORAL COMMUNICATION ON ITEMS NOT ON THE AGENDA

NONE

5.  DISCUSSION ITEMS

A.  SUSTAINABILITY ELEMENT - BASELINE CONDITIONS

Planning Manager Naughton stated that the Sustainability Element is possible through a grant
provided by the Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG) and in attendance is
India Brookover, Project Manager, SCAG. The consulting team consists of Laura Male and
Jonathan Cain with Sapphos Environmental and Ryan Johnson with Alta Planning.

Jonathan Cain, Sapphos Environmental provided an overview of the items that will be discussed.
He began the meeting with the results of the Sustainability Survey with the first question – What
does sustainability mean to you? The most common occurring themes were future, environment,
resources, water, healthy, generations, among others.

Mr. Cain asked the Committee Member to vote for one of the definitions for sustainability. The
choices were as follows:

  1. Creating community practices, policies and economic programs that improve quality of life
  by addressing energy, water, mobility and land use needs while decreasing waste and
  emissions to ensure the property of future generations in the City of Rolling Hills Estates.

  2. Creating community practices, policies, and economic programs that improve quality of
  life for future generations in the City of Rolling Hills Estates.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  1
 MINUTES, MARCH 8, 2021
   3. Balancing environmental conservation, social responsibility, and economic prosperity to
  meet our personal needs while ensuring he ability of future generations to meet their
  needs.

There were three votes for definition 3 and two votes for definition 2.

Mr. Cain provided an overview of relevant programs and regulations for each of the seven
sustainability pillars, which include, Air Quality and GHG, Waste Management and Recycling,
Water Resources, Energy, Mobility, Lane Use and Quality of Life.

Mr. Cain provided an overview of the existing Sustainability Programs implemented by the City.

Mr. Cain provided a summary of the analysis for each of the sustainability pillars.

Air Quality and GHG: The primary source of air pollution in the City is from vehicles. The largest
contributors to GHG emissions are vehicles and energy. The data is gathered from the nearest
air quality monitoring stations, two which are located in Long Beach and one in Signal Hill. In
previous meetings, there recommendations to implement a monitoring system within the City and
this will be explored. The Sustainability Element goals have been built with existing emissions
targets in mind. SCAG has a stated GHG emissions reduction target of 19 percent by 2035 from
2005 emissions levels. The City has its own GHG Emission reduction goal of 80 percent below
1990 levels by 2050.

The Sustainability Pillar Goals for Air Quality and GHG include: 1) Reduce greenhouse gas
emissions; 2) Reduce air pollutant emissions; 3) Assess climate threat; 4) Prepare for long-term
adaptability; 5) Prepare for short-term hazards; 6) Manage heat island effects.

Waste Management and Recycling: Waste Management and Recycling baseline conditions
showed that the average resident threw away 4 pounds of solid waste per day in 2015, which is
a reduction from 2007, when the average resident threw away an average of 9 pounds of solid
waste per day. The City disposed approximately 9,800 tons of solid waste in 2019. Approximately
80 percent of this went to the Sobrante landfill. Sobrante has a remaining capacity of almost 4
million cubic yards and is projected to remain in operation through 2047. This may be an area
that warrants a more aggressive approach when establishing the Sustainability Element’s waste
management and recycling goals. The baseline analysis shows that the City has already achieved
a 50 percent reduction in the generation of solid waste through the Greener Path Program.
The Sustainability Pillar Goals for Waste Management and Recyling include: 1) Support
sustainable procurement practices; 2) Use recycled materials; 3) Use regional materials; 4) Divert
waste from landfills; 5) Provide for deconstruction and recycling; 6) Reduce net embodied energy.

Water Resources: A baseline profile of the water resources found in the City include: surface
waters, surface water, a portion of the West Coast Subbasin of the Los Angeles Groundwater
Basin Coastal Plan, and imported water from the Metropolitan Water District of Southern
California. Cal Water estimates that it can meet the Palos Verdes District water demands through
2040. Existing policies to be built on include: Water Shortage and Water Shortage Management
Plan, Ahwahnee Water Principles for Resource-Efficient Communities Program, and Water
Efficient Landscape Ordinance (No. 658).

The Sustainability Pillar Goals for Water Resources include: 1) Protect freshwater availability; 2)
Reduce potable water consumption; 3) Monitor water systems; 4) Protect wetlands and surface
water; 5) Manage stormwater; 6) Prevent surface and groundwater contamination; 7) Maintain
wetland and surface water functions.

Energy: The primary sources for energy in the City are natural gas and electricity; it is also
important to note the impact energy use has on the community. The City’s electricity use
accounted for approximately 11 percent of all municipal GHG emissions in 2012. GHG emissions
in 2012 totaled almost 72,000 mega tons of CO2 equivalent. Sixty-two percent of the total
emissions came from residential energy use, and 47 percent came from City electricity and natural
gas use. It is also important to note that energy use overall is declining, except for natural gas
usage, which remains steady. This decline is most likely due to existing programs the City
participates in like the Sierra Club Cool Cities Program and the HERO program.

CHAIR STEGURA asked if there is a breakout of electricity and natural gas emissions separately.
Mr. Cain stated that they do have that information and will be part of the document on baseline
conditions.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  2
 MINUTES, MARCH 8, 2021
 Planning Manager Naughton stated it is important to note that the electricity is delivered by
Southern California Edison (SCE) in the City, but the actual generation comes through Clean
Power Alliance (CPA).

The Sustainability Pillar Goals for Energy include: 1) Reduce energy consumption; 2) Use
renewable energy; 3) Commission and monitor energy systems.

Ryan Johnson, Alta Planning provided the presentation on baseline conditions for mobility.

Mobility: The Mobility Element focuses on Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) and trying to reduce the
amount of driving in and to the City, but other elements of the transportation system are being
considered. These include: the make-up of the transportation fleet, what kind of vehicles are being
driven in the private and transit fleet. Data from PV transit, Metro and LADOT (who runs a
Commuter Express bus) to get a sense of their long-term policies for reducing the number of fossil
fuel burning buses in the fleet. Also identified are existing transportation facilities in the City,
including the public transportation system, bicycle facilities, pedestrian facilities, equestrian
facilities. These will be looked at to see how they can be maximized and expanded to help reduce
local trips. Consideration for sustainability in transportation a life cycle cost for roadway materials,
such as asphalt and paving. There are examples of communities around the world using more
sustainable materials and incorporating green infrastructure as part of sustainability efforts.

The Sustainability Pillar Goals for Mobility include: 1) Improve community mobility and access; 2)
Encourage alternate modes of transportation; 3) Improve site accessibility, safety, and wayfinding.

Jonathan Cain provided the presentation on baseline conditions for land use.

Land Use: Approximately 60 percent of the City’s land use is residential, and 39% is commercial,
public, and recreational land use combined. There is less than 1% of undeveloped land in the
City. The majority of what is developed exists in low-density neighborhoods. The baseline analysis
creates many opportunities to address land issues, such as connectivity and one of the most
commonly mentioned themes is local character.

The Sustainability Pillar Goals for Land Use include: 1) Preserve prime habitat; 2) Preserve
greenfields; 3) Reduce pesticide and fertilizer impacts; 4) Preserve species biodiversity; 5) Control
invasive species; 6) Restore disturbed soils.

Quality of Life: The most common goal recommendations received was about maintaining the
City’s unique, semi-rural character. Another existing baseline condition to consider is that
residents are well served by open space, trails, and quality parks. Primary employment sectors in
the City are retail, food, education, and professional services. Residents have good access to
food, in terms of local grocery stores. Regional traffic and noise were presented as a hinderance
to quality of life.

The Sustainability Pillar Goals for Quality of Life include: 1) Improve community quality of life; 2)
Stimulate sustainable growth and development; 3) Develop local skills and capabilities; 4)
Enhance public health and safety; 5) Minimize noise and vibration; 6) Minimize light pollution; 7)
Preserve cultural and historic resources; 8) Preserve views and local character; 9) Enhance public
space.

Laura Male, Sapphos Environmental, provided an overview of the next steps for development of
the Sustainability Element. The next step will be assembling community comments that have been
received through an interactive map website. The existing conditions presentation will be provided
to the Stakeholder list that has been prepared with the City at the end of March. The next EAC
Meeting will be held on April 7, 2021 and the anticipated public review of the Draft Sustainability
Element in August 2021.

6.  CONSULTANT/STAFF ITEMS/COMMITTEE ITEMS

In response to a question by COMMITTEE MEMBER O’MALLEY, Mr. Cain stated that in terms
of Quality of Life, the analysis was a feedback item that traffic congestion, while limited
comparatively within the City, is still perceived as a quality of life issue. In relation to Air Quality
and GHG, yes, the primary sources of GHG and air pollution are from automobiles.

CHAIR STEGURA asked if having an air quality monitoring station in the City, considering the
proximity to the ocean, would have more favorable readings. Mr. Cain stated that he liked the
idea and in order to get a good data it should be done more locally.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  3
 MINUTES, MARCH 8, 2021
 COMMITTEE MEMBER CHAN-SOUTHWELL asked if the survey results would be provided. Mr.
Cain stated that these could be provided at the next meeting.

The Committee discussed sharing the Community Input map to help get more feedback from the
community.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI requested additional consideration of graywater use for
Rolling Hills Estates Golf Course. Planning Manager Naughton stated that she will reach out to
the neighbor golf course in Palos Verdes (which has purple pipes for graywater irrigation).

Planning Manager Naughton asked if a multiple-choice survey would be more effective. The EAC
agreed and requested an extension for the input deadline if an additional survey was provided.

7.  ADJOURNMENT

CHAIR STEGURA adjourned the meeting at 7:20 p.m. The next meeting will be held on April 7,
2021 at 6:00 p.m. via video teleconference.
